entry.title: Steam machine
entry.content:
I built my first gaming PC with my dad when I was 13 in ~2009.

Before that I was using a bunch of really low powered laptops and desktops that didn't have dedicated graphics and were certified for Windows 98 so you know... they barely connected to the internet.

Building a PC really is just like complex legos, but much like building Ikea furniture, the fact that I had a hand in building this machine made me way more invested in it's operation and empowered me to fix, tinker, and upgrade it over the years.

On top of building though I also sort of designed the machine, choosing the parts, double checking that everything would fit together and was compatible, and finding a good deal for everything, forced me to have a deeper knowledge of the machine.

It was fun to assemble this complex device and then to be able to play any game I could want on the pretty budget hardware, around $1,000 all told at the time.

The PC served me well, going through a few rounds of upgrades including graphics cards, hard drive expansion, and every other generation of Windows.

In 2023 I bought a Steam Deck to help me play games in my increasingly sparse free time. I would still turn my PC on from time to time, but seeing as it's core purpose was Gaming hardware, and I wasn't playing games on it very much, it gathered dust.

After a few months of not being turned on, I decided to shelve the tower all together. Between work laptop, my Linux laptop for personal projects, and the Deck for gaming, I didn't have a need for it.

During this time I was also being "radicalized" (with the most luke-warm hot-take) that Windows sucked so bad I just shouldn't use it at all.

10 years ago Windows might be considered a "necessary evil" for a PC gamer. In that decade though it has gotten much worse injecting ads, AI, and just buggy core software into a product that was just OK to start with.

Thankfully, Valve has been building up an ecosystem of software to play Windows games on Linux so well that it Just Works (TM) -- something I never would have said about anything Linux related when I was 13.

So here I was at the start of 2026: an avid gamer without a gaming PC, a traveler adrift, limited by the hardware. The Deck was nice, but had it's rough edges; while it could technically play all of my games, it would need to be on the absolutely lowest settings for newer titles which was tolerable but frustrating.

The Steam Machine really did answer all of my needs. It was a PC in a small form-factor, promised 4k 60fps performance on most games, and was designed for the console gamer audience. The day it was announced, I entered myself into the queue and a few months later got it in the mail.

Honestly, it's not revolutionary -- or at least none of it feels revolutionary.

  • The software just feels like SteamOS, if you have a Steam Deck it feels exactly the same.
  • The Steam Controller also feels like a Deck with the screen cut out.
  • Performance has been a totally non-issue. I only use 1080p monitors and every game I've run works out the box with awesome performance.

Especially if you are a 1080p monitor kinda guy, this really does feel like a PC-console experience we've been promised.

Before this I didn't really have a "Couch Gaming" setup. When I had the gaming PC, that was also a workstation so I needed a desk to work at. And my Deck can connect to a TV but it only supports 720p which like... even I have standards. We also don't have a standard living room couch + TV for setup that I grew up with to encourage the kids toward non-tv activities like reading and playing.

So I took this as an opportunity to setup a small gaming nook with a couch, small monitor, Steam Machine, and speakers. As much as I still love gaming on the Deck, it has been really nice to sit back and veg out in a way that I haven't since I was a kid playing xbox 360 at my parents house.

Is the Steam Machine good? Yes. It is delivering on exactly what I feel it promised. If you are a PC gamer with a sizeable steam library, and you don't yet have a couch gaming setup, but you want one, you should check it out. The device is small and sleek, very quiet, and again Just Works (TM) in a way I never would have expected from a Linux PC 13 years ago.

entry.title: the xteink4 got me reading again
entry.content:
A few weeks ago I bought the xteink4 on a whim based on a co-worker's suggestion. Best $60 I've spent in a looong time.

What makes it awesome

I carry this thing around with me all day every day and I have been reading waaay more than before. Let's get into why.

I am busy so convenience is king

Between family, friends, job, exercising, and sleeping I have maaaaybe 2 hours a day to myself if I'm lucky. That time though is usually spent playing games, writing this blog, or hacking on a game -- things that require sitting down at a desk and focusing for a block of time.

I've found that when I lower the barrier to entry for a task, I usually start doing it more.

  • Not blogging enough? I built editor.elijah.run so I can blog from my phone.
  • Not gaming enough? I bought a steamdeck.
  • Not reading enough? That's where the xteink4 comes in bay-bee!

I'm able to keep this device with me literally at all times. It slips in my bag right next to my phone, barely taking up any space. The battery seems to never die, lasting well over a week, so it's low maintenance. Those together mean I can turn it on, read what would be the equivalent of 1-2 pages, and put it away without skipping a beat.

Sure I can carry some small books around with me all day, just in case I get a few minutes to read one or two pages, but it's size is nice because regardless of the size of the book I will have it with me 24/7.

Thriving open source community

One surprise upside to this device was finding that it had a huge and thriving ecosystem of firmware hackers -- mainly readme.club. Custom firmware, sharing background images, and just a vibrant community of excited users was a real happy accident on my part -- I just got it because it was cheap(ish) and I don't love my Kindle.

I'm currently using the most common (non-stock) firmware: crosspoint which I still can't get over that you can just... load firmware onto this thing using a webpage... we really do live in the future.

It's shockingly easy to flash new and even custom firmware on the xteink, which is exciting! I might even vibe-code my own with Rust -- I've been wanting a good flashcard app and this seems like a good device for that...

Downsides

It's not all perfect, but the downsides are [for me] easy enough to overlook.

DRM Free epubs are hard to find [legally]

I am really sad at how difficult it is to get an epub for a device like this. I tried purchasing and downloading a book from ~3 online ebook retailers and each of them had some DRM scheme that was way above my pay grade.

There are of course tons of sites you can use to download epubs if you just search "X book epub", so there are ways to get what you want to read on this thing, but it's sad that there's no legal way to get many books onto the device.

Before this I was an avid Libby user, getting almost all of my reading from the library. Sure you have to wait a few weeks for the popular stuff, but I'm a slow ready so that wasn't an issue. I wish there was some way to load Libby books onto this, and maybe with custom firmware there is, but not that I could find in 2026.

There are some custom firmware that support alternative formats, like markdown, so you could in theory use this to read blogs, emails, whatever! It's just a small e-ink screen with a wireless connection running a binary blob!

[Debatable] missing features

Software fixes most issues, but there are also some hardware features of the hardware I should mention.

  1. There is no backlight. This isn't a deal breaker for me, but I do enjoy the backlight on my Kindle Paperwhite. It's difficult not being able to read in bed without waking up my partner.
  2. No touchscreen. This is a feature for me, but everything is controlled by one of the 7 buttons (1 power, 3 rockers). It's a little clunky at first, but it's nice not accidentally turning the page as much as I do on the touchscreen Kindles.

Over all I really like this thing. I've been reading way more than before due mostly to the fact that I can have it everywhere, so any time I can fit 5 minutes of reading into my day it's there and I don't have any excuses.
